title: Sukesha says, I don't know
hookLine: the last two students ask about om and about a person made of sixteen parts, and one of them admits he once had to say, I don't know
carry: satya: i don't know is better than a lie
tomorrow: is there one thing that makes everything make sense?
last: THE ATMAN IS THE SEER, EVEN IN SLEEP.

lines: DO YOU KNOW THE SIXTEEN PARTS?
A LIE DRIES UP TO THE ROOT.
cards: Sukesha, the sixth student, opens with a story against himself. A prince of Kosala once came to me, he says, and asked: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I said, I don't know.
If I knew, why wouldn't I tell you? Whoever speaks what isn't true dries up to the root, so I can't speak falsely. The prince got into his chariot without a word, and left.
Now, Sukesha says to Pippalada, I'm asking you. Where is that person?

teach.h: OM: THE HIGHER AND THE LOWER.
teach.b: First, the fifth question, from Satyakama. What does a person win who meditates on om until the end of life? Pippalada says om is both the higher and the lower Brahman, and its sounds open different worlds.
Meditate on one of its three sounds, and you come quickly back to the human world. On two, and you go to the world of the moon, and return.

teach.h: LIKE A SNAKE OUT OF ITS SKIN.
teach.b: But one who meditates on all three, the whole of om, is freed from wrong the way a snake slips out of its old skin. Then Sukesha's question.

teach.h: SIXTEEN PARTS, FROM BREATH TO NAME.
teach.b: Where is the person of sixteen parts? Right here, Pippalada says, inside the body. And he tells how the sixteen arise.
The self thought: when I leave, who will leave with me? It made breath. From breath, faith.
Then space, wind, light, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food, strength. Then discipline, sacred verses, action, the worlds, and finally, name.
Sixteen: everything a life is made of. Then an image.

teach.h: RIVERS REACH THE SEA AND LOSE THEIR NAMES.
teach.b: As rivers flowing toward the sea reach it and disappear, their names and shapes broken up, and people simply say, the sea, so these sixteen parts reach the person and disappear. Their names are gone.
And that one is without parts, and deathless. The six students honored Pippalada: you are our father, who carries us across our ignorance to the farther shore. And remember how Sukesha began.

That's the teaching under the whole scene: satya, truthfulness, sits near the top of Hindu ethics, and a student of Brahman would rather say I don't know than speak falsely, because a lie dries a person up to the root.

how: Om is commonly chanted at the start and close of Hindu prayer and study, and some teachers use the Prashna's line about a lie drying a person up to the root when they speak about truthfulness.

games.q: the last two questions — tap the pairs.

s: Sukesha pretended to know the answer to impress the prince
he said, I don't know: a lie dries a person up to the root.
the text says the person of sixteen parts is right here, in the body
Pippalada: right here, within, is that person.
the students end by calling Pippalada their father
who carries them across ignorance to the farther shore.

games.q: you're Sukesha. a prince asks you a question you can't answer. what do you say?
o: make something up; he'll never check.
I don't know. if I knew, I'd tell you.
that's a secret I can't share.
games.why: Sukesha said plainly, I don't know, because whoever speaks untruth dries up to the root. the prince left in silence.

practice: Begin where the list of sixteen begins: one breath in, one breath out.
Then let a few of the others pass through your attention, in no hurry: faith, the space around you, the warmth of the body, the food you ate, the work of your hands, and last of all, your name.
Don't hold on to any of it; come back to the breath, and stay there.

wordCard.voice: Q5 and 6, the last two questions. Om opens the higher and lower worlds; the person of sixteen parts is right here, and the parts return to it like rivers to the sea.

orig.note: Sanskrit ṣoḍaśa-kala, of sixteen parts: the person Sukesha asks about in Prashna 6.

carryVoice: Your line: satya. I don't know is better than a lie. Tomorrow, a new Upanishad splits all knowing in two. That's day four hundred ten.
